verdict.rationale: The pattern of words across law, wisdom, gospel, and epistle condemns the parts that make up the practice, namely the deliberate look aimed at sexual desire, sexual immorality (porneia), the controlling passion of lust, and the dishonoring use of the body. Matthew 5:28 reads, in transliterated Greek, 'pas ho blepon gynaika pros to epithymesai auten ede emoicheusen auten en te kardia autou', meaning 'everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart'. The present active participle 'blepon' (the one looking, an ongoing action) joined to the articular infinitive of purpose 'pros to epithymesai' (in order to desire her) names a look whose aim is lust. The aorist 'emoicheusen' (a completed past action meaning 'he committed adultery') paired with the adverb 'ede' (already) and the locative phrase 'en te kardia' (in the heart) fixes the guilt as already complete before any outward act. 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 makes 'hagiasmos' (sanctification, being set apart for God) the 'thelema' (will) of God, defined as 'apechesthai apo tes porneias' (to keep abstaining from sexual immorality) and refusing 'pathos epithymias' (the passion of lust) 'kathaper ta ethne ta me eidota ton theon' (just as the nations that do not know God), with the body kept 'en hagiasmo kai time' (in sanctification and honor). 1 Corinthians 6:18 commands 'pheugete ten porneian' (flee sexual immorality). Job 31:1 records 'berith karatti le einay' (a covenant I cut with my eyes), so as not to gaze 'al bethulah' (upon a young woman). Psalm 101:3 vows 'lo ashit le neged einay devar beliyaal' (I will not set before my eyes a worthless or wicked thing). The convergence of the inner extension of the Ten Commandments, the wisdom discipline of the eye, and the Pauline ethic of sanctification, all on the same point (the desiring look that engages illicit sexual interest), is what makes the verdict decisive rather than disputed.

scripture.reasoning: The Greek reads 'Ekousate hoti errethe, ou moicheuseis', which means 'you heard that it was said, you shall not commit adultery'. The future indicative form 'moicheuseis' (a future statement of fact, from 'moicheuo', to commit adultery) recites the seventh commandment of Exodus 20:14 and Deuteronomy 5:18 as the inherited prohibition. Jesus cites the external statute as the foil against which he will extend the prohibition inward in verse 28. The verse establishes that the baseline standard under discussion is adultery itself, not a lesser matter.

The Greek reads 'Ego de lego hymin hoti pas ho blepon gynaika pros to epithymesai auten ede emoicheusen auten en te kardia autou', meaning 'but I say to you that everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart'. The present active participle 'blepon' (the one looking, an ongoing action) is qualified by the articular infinitive of purpose 'pros to epithymesai' (in order to desire her), naming not an accidental glance but a look whose aim is lust. The aorist indicative 'emoicheusen' (a completed past action meaning 'committed adultery') paired with the adverb 'ede' (already) and the locative phrase 'en te kardia' (in the heart) declares the guilt complete before any outward act. The construction places the moral violation precisely at the point of intentional, desiring looking, which is the defining act of the practice under examination.

The Greek reads 'Touto gar estin thelema tou theou, ho hagiasmos hymon, apechesthai hymas apo tes porneias', meaning 'for this is the will of God, your sanctification, that you abstain from sexual immorality'. The predicate nominative chain (a 'X is Y' equating construction) identifies the 'thelema' (will) of God with 'hagiasmos' (sanctification, being set apart for God), then explicates it with the present middle infinitive 'apechesthai' (to keep abstaining, an ongoing action) governed by 'apo tes porneias' (from sexual immorality). 'Porneia' (sexual immorality) is the broad noun covering the whole field of illicit sexual activity, and the durative infinitive (an ongoing infinitive) makes abstention an ongoing state, not a single decision. Sanctification is defined negatively as continuous distance from 'porneia' (sexual immorality).

The Greek reads 'Eidenai hekaston hymon to heautou skeuos ktasthai en hagiasmo kai time', meaning 'that each of you know how to gain control of his own vessel in sanctification and honor'. The distributive 'hekaston' (each one) makes the command individual. The present infinitive 'ktasthai' (to gain control of, to possess) takes 'to heautou skeuos' (his own vessel, either the body or the marital relation) as object, governed by the dual prepositional phrase 'en hagiasmo kai time' (in sanctification and honor). 'Time' (honor) is the antonym of degrading treatment of the body or of another person. The positive command frames the body and the sexual capacity as something to be held in honor, which the degrading consumption of illicit sexual imagery directly violates.

The Greek reads 'Me en pathei epithymias kathaper kai ta ethne ta me eidota ton theon', meaning 'not in the passion of lust just as the nations that do not know God'. The prohibition 'me en pathei epithymias' (not in the passion of lust) names the inner disposition forbidden, with 'pathos' (a controlling passion, a rare term, occurring only three times in the entire Bible, at Romans 1:26, Colossians 3:5, and 1 Thessalonians 4:5) denoting an overpowering emotion and 'epithymias' (of lust, of strong desire) as its content. The comparison 'kathaper kai ta ethne ta me eidota ton theon' (just as the nations that do not know God) marks lust-driven sexual conduct as the mark of those outside the knowledge of God, the inverse of 'hagiasmos' (sanctification). The verse couples illicit sexual desire with ignorance of God, placing it categorically outside sanctified conduct.

The Greek reads 'Pheugete ten porneian', meaning 'flee sexual immorality'. The present active imperative 'pheugete' (keep fleeing, an ongoing command) paired with the definite article 'ten porneian' (the sexual immorality) governs the whole category of illicit sexual activity, with the article generalizing 'porneia' (sexual immorality) as a whole rather than naming a single act. The continuous-aspect imperative (an ongoing command) makes flight the standing posture toward 'porneia' (sexual immorality), not a one-time decision. The verse stands as the most concise positive Pauline command on the category and corroborates 1 Thessalonians 4:3.

The Hebrew reads 'Berith karatti le einay umah etbonen al bethulah', meaning 'a covenant I cut with my eyes, so how could I gaze upon a young woman'. The idiom 'karath berith' (to cut a covenant) is the standard Hebrew formula for binding oneself by oath (over 80 such pairings in the Bible), here applied to 'einayim' (the eyes) as the organ of desiring sight. The hithpolel (a Hebrew reflexive-intensive form) 'etbonen' (from 'bin', to perceive) means to gaze attentively or consider closely, and the rhetorical 'umah' (so how) treats such a gaze as a covenant breach. The ETCBC database (a syntactic database of the Hebrew Bible) marks the clause as a question (Ques) functioning to deny. Job locates moral self-government precisely at the controlled use of the eyes toward the female object of potential lust, the same act Matthew 5:28 condemns.

The Hebrew reads 'Lo ashit le neged einay devar beliyaal', meaning 'I will not set before my eyes a worthless or wicked thing'. The imperfect 'ashit' (I will set, an ongoing or future action) negated by 'lo' (not) expresses settled resolve, and 'le neged einay' (before my eyes) makes the visual field the object of moral guarding. 'Devar beliyaal' (a thing of 'beliyaal', that is, worthlessness or wickedness) names whatever is morally corrupting placed before the sight. The verse establishes a positive discipline of refusing corrupting things before the eyes, the direct counterpart to deliberately viewing illicit sexual material.

The Hebrew reads 'Lo tinaph', meaning 'you shall not commit adultery'. This is the seventh word of the Ten Commandments using the qal (the simple active form of the Hebrew verb) imperfect of 'naaph' (the Hebrew verb of adultery), negated by 'lo' (not). The Septuagint (the Greek Old Testament) renders this as 'ou moicheuseis' with 'moicheuo' (to commit adultery), which is the exact verb Jesus cites in Matthew 5:27 and the same verb he applies to the heart act in 5:28, demonstrating continuity between the external statute and the interior extension.

The Hebrew reads 'Al tahmod yafyah bilvavekha ve al tiqqahaka be afappeyha', meaning 'do not desire her beauty in your heart, nor let her capture you with her eyelids'. The jussive (a Hebrew form expressing wish or command) 'al tahmod' (do not covet, from 'hamad', the verb of the tenth commandment) takes 'yafyah' (her beauty) as object and 'bilvavekha' (in your heart) as the location, exactly paralleling Matthew 5:28 'en te kardia' (in the heart). The second clause warns against capture 'be afappeyha' (by her eyelids, the visual lure). Wisdom literature already locates the sin in the heart-level desire provoked through the eyes, confirming the Matthean reading is a development of an existing canonical pattern.

The Greek reads 'Nekrosate oun ta mele ta epi tes ges, porneian, akatharsian, pathos, epithymian kaken, kai ten pleonexian', meaning 'therefore put to death the members that are on the earth, sexual immorality, impurity, passion, evil desire, and greed'. The aorist active imperative 'nekrosate' (put to death, a completed-action command) governs an asyndetic list (a list without joining words) whose first four items overlap exactly with the 1 Thessalonians 4:3-5 vocabulary, 'porneia' (sexual immorality) plus 'pathos' (controlling passion) plus 'epithymia' (lust). The same Pauline triad applied to a different audience confirms that the cluster of words is not local to Thessalonica, it is the standing Pauline category.

complicating_texts.resolution: The stem says pornography use is sin, but the word pornography names a modern technology and does not occur in the Bible. One could object that the word anchors address adultery, fornication, and gazing at actual persons, not viewing images. Resolution, Matthew 5:28 fixes guilt at the point of 'blepon pros to epithymesai' (looking in order to lust), and the object of the look (gynaika, a woman) is the same morally whether the woman is physically present or depicted. The morally relevant act named by the verb plus the purpose infinitive is the intentional engagement of sexual desire through sight, which is identically present when the object is a depicted person. The pattern of words condemns the constituent act regardless of medium.

'Skeuos' (vessel) is ambiguous in its sense between the man's own body (the dominant Greek metaphor, compare 2 Corinthians 4:7) and his wife (a possible Hebraic idiom). If 'skeuos' (vessel) means wife, one might restrict verse 4 to acquiring a spouse honorably and read it as silent on solitary viewing. Resolution, either reading supports the verdict. If 'skeuos' (vessel) is the body, the command to possess it 'en hagiasmo kai time' (in sanctification and honor) forbids degrading sexual use. If it is the wife, the command to hold the marital relation in honor is corroded by 'porneia' (sexual immorality) and 'pathos epithymias' (the passion of lust), which verses 3 and 5 forbid in any case. The surrounding 'apechesthai apo tes porneias' (to abstain from sexual immorality) and 'me en pathei epithymias' (not in the passion of lust) carry the verdict independent of the 'skeuos' (vessel) decision.

Job 31:1 is a personal vow within a self-imprecation oath (an oath calling down curse on oneself), and one might say it expresses one righteous man's private scruple rather than a universal norm. Resolution, the clause uses the formal covenant idiom 'karath berith' (to cut a covenant), the strongest available binding language in biblical Hebrew, and the rhetorical question 'umah etbonen' (so how could I gaze) treats the desiring gaze as self-evidently a covenant breach for the upright. The wisdom genre presents Job's standard as exemplary, and Proverbs 6:25 generalizes the same heart-and-eye dynamic into instruction. The vow form does not weaken the lexical witness that the desiring look is morally culpable.

A second possible reading of 'pas ho blepon gynaika pros to epithymesai auten' (everyone looking at a woman in order to lust for her) takes 'pros' plus articular infinitive as result rather than purpose, yielding 'so as to lust for her'. The result reading would broaden the rule to include the involuntary involvement of desire as well as deliberate desiring. Resolution, the purpose sense is the strongly attested default for 'pros' plus articular infinitive in Koine Greek, and either reading supports the verdict in the case of pornography. Deliberate viewing of sexual imagery satisfies the purpose reading directly, and even more so satisfies the broader result reading. The verdict is robust across both lexically defensible glosses of the construction.

variant_units_examined.note: Some manuscript witnesses omit or relocate 'auten' (her) after 'epithymesai' (to lust), and a few read 'pros to epithymesai autes'. The verb 'moicheuo' (to commit adultery) paired with the locative 'en te kardia' (in the heart) and the participle 'blepon' (the one looking) is uniformly attested across the manuscript tradition, so the verdict that the desiring look is heart adultery is unaffected.

The referent of 'skeuos' (vessel, that is, body versus wife) is debated as a matter of glossing, but the manuscript text is stable. The surrounding 'apechesthai apo tes porneias' (to abstain from sexual immorality) and 'me en pathei epithymias' (not in the passion of lust) secure the verdict regardless of how 'skeuos' (vessel) is glossed.

variants.note: No ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) was examined for these verses, and no load-bearing textual decision rests on a contested variant. The Greek anchors lie outside the 3 John CBGM sample (the Coherence-Based Genealogical Method dataset), so the status is shadow.

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Jesus takes 'ou moicheuseis' (you shall not commit adultery) and relocates the violation to 'blepon pros to epithymesai' (looking in order to lust), the intentional desiring look, with 'ede emoicheusen' (he has already committed adultery) marking completed guilt in the heart. The defining act of the practice is precisely this look.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: Wisdom ethics of the guarded eye (Job 31.1, Ps 101.3, Prov 6.25)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Job cuts a 'berith' (covenant) with his eyes against gazing, the psalmist refuses 'devar beliyaal' (a worthless or wicked thing) before his eyes, and Proverbs forbids desiring beauty in the heart and capture by the eyelids. The wisdom corpus already disciplines the eye as the gateway to illicit desire.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: Pauline sanctification ethic (1 Thess 4.3-5, 1 Cor 6.18, Col 3.5)
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: 'Hagiasmos' (sanctification) is the 'thelema' (will) of God, defined as 'apechesthai apo tes porneias' (to abstain from sexual immorality) and refusing 'pathos epithymias' (the passion of lust), with the body held 'en time' (in honor). Lust-driven sexual conduct is marked as the way of 'ta ethne ta me eidota ton theon' (the nations that do not know God), the opposite of sanctification. 1 Corinthians 6:18 commands 'pheugete ten porneian' (flee sexual immorality), and Colossians 3:5 lists the same 'porneia' (sexual immorality), 'pathos' (controlling passion), 'epithymia' (lust) triad.

competing_lens_verdicts.framework: Narrow medium objection (the object of view is a depicted person, not the looker is neighbor)
competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: partially complicates but does not overturn
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: A reader could press that Matthew 5:28 names 'gynaika' (a woman) as the object of the look, suggesting a known person, and that Job 31:1 names 'bethulah' (a young woman) as a real young woman in proximity. The strongest form of this lens reads the prohibition as restricted to looking at one's potential neighbor with intent to act, not to interaction with images. The lexical answer is that the participial construction 'blepon' (the one looking) plus purpose infinitive 'epithymesai' (to lust) locates the guilt in the looker's internal aim, not in the relational status of the object, and Paul forbids the inner state 'pathos epithymias' (the passion of lust) itself in 1 Thessalonians 4:5, independent of who provoked it. The lens does not survive the grammar.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict turns on the convergence of inner extension of the Ten Commandments, wisdom discipline of the eye, and Pauline sanctification ethics. The term pornography is post-canonical (not present in the Bible), so the lexical case proceeds by identifying the practice's constituent acts (the desiring look, 'porneia' or sexual immorality, the passion of lust, the dishonoring of the body) and showing each is condemned across the canon. Progressive revelation is in play in that Matthew 5:28 makes explicit and interior what the seventh and tenth commandments and the wisdom literature already pointed toward.

stem_audit.neutralized_form: Does the lexical pattern of the canon treat deliberate looking aimed at sexual desire, sexual immorality ('porneia'), the passion of lust, and the dishonoring of the body and marriage as sin.
stem_audit.notes: VERDICT-CHANGED: The stem asserts the verdict (pornography use is sin) and supplies three rationales (heart adultery, exploitation, corrosion of the marriage bed). The word pornography itself is a modern term absent from the canon (descended morphologically from 'porneia' (sexual immorality) plus 'grapho' (to write or depict), so literally the writing or depicting of porneia), so the stem is verdict-loaded relative to the lexical store and must be neutralized to its constituent acts. The word anchors directly address the desiring look (Matthew 5:28), 'porneia' (sexual immorality) and the passion of lust (1 Thessalonians 4:3-5, 1 Corinthians 6:18, Colossians 3:5), and the guarding of the eyes (Job 31:1, Psalm 101:3, Proverbs 6:25). The exploitation of persons in the industry and the corrosion of the marriage bed are downstream moral and sociological claims that the lexical store does not directly measure, so the verdict rests on the heart adultery and 'porneia' (sexual immorality) strands, which are unambiguous, rather than on the exploitation or marriage corrosion clauses. The verdict is derived on the original stem but anchored only where the lexical evidence speaks.

lay_summary: The question asks whether using pornography is sin. The word pornography is modern and does not appear in the Bible, so the lexical work first identifies the constituent acts of the practice (the desiring look at a person depicted for sexual interest, the engagement of sexual immorality, the use of the body apart from honor) and then asks what the original languages say about each. The clearest text is Matthew 5 verses 27 and 28. Jesus repeats the old command, you shall not commit adultery, and then says that everyone who looks at a woman in order to lust for her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. The grammar is decisive. The present participle for looking (blepon) is governed by a purpose construction meaning in order to desire (pros to epithymesai), so the verse does not address an accidental glance but a look whose aim is lust. The verb for committed adultery stands in the aorist (a completed past action, emoicheusen) with the adverb already (ede), marking the guilt as complete, and the locative phrase fixes the act in the heart (en te kardia). The text places the moral violation precisely at the deliberate desiring look, which is the defining act of viewing sexual images. Paul ties the same vocabulary together in 1 Thessalonians 4 verses 3 to 5, where the will of God is sanctification (hagiasmos), defined as continuing to abstain from sexual immorality (porneia) and refusing to live in the passion of lust (pathos epithymias) like the nations that do not know God. Porneia is a broad word covering the whole field of illicit sexual activity, and 1 Corinthians 6 verse 18 commands flight from it as the sin against one's own body. Two wisdom texts discipline the eye directly. Job 31 verse 1 uses the strongest Hebrew oath idiom, to cut a covenant (karath berith), applied to the eyes, so as not to gaze on a young woman. Psalm 101 verse 3 refuses to set anything worthless before the eyes. Proverbs 6 verse 25 forbids desiring beauty in the heart and being captured by the eyelids, joining heart and eye exactly as Jesus does. The convergence is what makes this verdict decisive rather than disputed. Three independent strands of the canon, the Decalogue extended by Jesus, the wisdom guarding of the eye, and the Pauline sanctification ethic, all locate the sin at the same juncture, the intentional look that engages sexual desire and the indulgence of porneia. Readers who hesitate to call viewing such images sin usually argue that the depicted person is not the looker's own neighbor, or that an image is not a person. The lexical objection is answered inside the text. Matthew 5 verse 28 fixes guilt at the look aimed at lust, not at any subsequent action toward the woman, and Paul forbids the passion itself, regardless of how it is provoked. On these grounds the lexical evidence affirms that the practice is sin.
